decision: The phone docs begin their own history: their first release is 0.1.0, and versions stay below 1.0 while the docs are still forming. The changelog and manifest inherited from the template they were made from are cleared, with a note saying whose history that was. Release-please reads its config and manifest.
why: The docs were made from text-as-data-template on 2026-11-04 and carried its history (1.0.0 to 1.2.0) as if their own; never released, release-please found no tag and proposed 1.0.0 - a claim of stability for docs days old and changing hourly. Found after landing: with no release at all, release-please treats the next as the first and gives it its own default, 1.0.0, whatever the manifest says; the config's initial-version (0.1.0) is what decides a first release.
rejected: Releasing 1.0.0 as proposed (promises what is not there); tagging 1.2.0 (it is the template's version, not the docs'); keeping the inherited changelog (it tells another repository's story as this one's).

decision: A part's status is derived (derive/support-status.sql, run through tad after every filing): broken where the latest run fails it; works where a test that proves the part does its work passed and none failed; otherwise what a person judged (judged, with the notes as its evidence). Each row says what the suite saw of the part and in which run (measured, measured_run); the tests table says what each test's pass proves - present or works.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: support status read off the suite's results, not typed. Tried beside the hand-written status first: read naively (a pass is works, nothing measured is unknown) it disagreed on 8 of 19 parts - a pass that only shows a part is there (the jack detector, Bluetooth powered, the modem seen, the NFC controller) is not the part working, and an absent measurement is no evidence against what was witnessed (the microphone's tries, fastboot). With proofs told apart, the rule and the judgment say the same on all 19.
rejected: Status typed by hand alone (it lags the phone: nothing turned it broken when a part failed); a pass read as works (would have called calls, SMS and NFC working with no SIM and no tag ever read); a measurement-less part read as unknown (would erase what was witnessed).

decision: linux-phone's pages (linux-phone-oco.github.io/docs) are its face, drawn in this place's CI from its open database: tad keeps and checks the data here; the family's other places are observed as the Linux Phones lens gathers them; the observatory's engine draws the face from that; tad's page of every table stands beside it under tables/. A landing here draws it again, and the clock every three hours, for what the other places land.
why: The author, 2026-11-17: the observatory's Linux Phones pages reflected real progress from CI and should be linux-phone's own face, with tad as the open database shared by the whole project, devlab filing the suite's results into it and the pages reflecting them - nobody drawing them by hand.
rejected: A copy of the observatory's pages kept here (a second renderer to drift); publishing from the lens's place (the database and its readers would live apart, and docs' address is the one already linked); the plain table index alone (it drew rows, not progress).

decision: The core of the project - making each part of a phone work - runs as its own session beside the conveyor's, from prompts/bring-up.md: it owns the kernel, the phone's hardware data, the upstream queue and the Sxmo profiles; the conveyor's session owns lab-tools, device-template and the face. Anything that changes the phone's state is done holding one lock (flock on ~/.local/state/devlab/CODENAME/phone.lock); each session works in clones of its own.
why: The author, 2026-11-17, asked for a parallel session on the actual core: research, reverse engineering, patches, delivered through the conveyor and proven by the suite. One phone and shared clones are where two sessions would undo each other (two jobs in one clone once merged each other's changes under one commit).
rejected: One session doing both (the conveyor kept pulling attention from the parts, and parts from the conveyor); two sessions without a lock or owners (a reboot under a kernel try, a reset clone).
